The eggs of Bombina bombina, which are deposited in shallow, ephemeral water bodies, are enveloped in a thick gelatinous matrix that provides thermal insulation and some protection from microbial infection. Upon hatching, which occurs after approximately seven days [ab = approximately seven days] at a constant incubation temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], the newly emerged tadpoles measure about 0.7 cm [Lb = about 0.7 cm] in total length. These early-stage larvae possess a modest wet weight of only 0.0017 grams [Wwb = 0.0017 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves allocated to each embryo. The initial period post-hatching is dominated by the absorption of endogenous yolk, during which the tadpoles remain largely inactive, adhering to submerged vegetation. This brief endotrophic phase is critical for the development of feeding structures and the onset of independent foraging. The relatively short embryonic development time aligns with observations from other Bombina species, suggesting a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid hatching to exploit transient breeding habitats before desiccation or predation pressure intensifies.

During the subsequent free-swimming larval stage, the tadpoles of the European fire-bellied toad exhibit considerable plasticity in growth rate, which is heavily modulated by water temperature. Under a thermal regime sustained at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the interval from hatching to the initiation of metamorphosis averages 70 days . At the onset of metamorphic climax, the tadpole has attained a total length of approximately 4.2 cm . Simultaneously, the developing toadlet at this point of transformation already measures 1.5 cm  in snout-vent length (SVL). The wet weight of the individual at this metamorphic transition has been recorded at 0.18 grams , a substantial increase from the hatchling mass. This developmental trajectory is punctuated by the resorption of the tail and the reorganisation of the digestive tract, which enables the transition from a herbivorous, filter-feeding existence to a terrestrial, carnivorous lifestyle as a juvenile froglet.

Following metamorphosis, the terrestrial juvenile phase is characterized by a period of sustained somatic growth and foraging activity. The time elapsed from the completion of metamorphosis to the attainment of sexual maturity has been documented as three years [tp = three years], when individuals are maintained at a mean environmental temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. At puberty, the toads have reached a snout-vent length of 4.0 cm [Lp = 4.0 cm] and a corresponding wet body mass of 4.1 grams [Wwp = 4.1 grams]. This maturation delay is typical of anurans inhabiting temperate regions, where a short active season and low metabolic rates slow the accumulation of the body reserves necessary for gonadal development. During this sub-adult phase, growth is most rapid in the first year after metamorphosis but decelerates as individuals approach their asymptotic size, reflecting a shift in energy allocation from somatic growth toward reproductive potential.

The maximum lifespan reported for Bombina bombina in the wild, again under a mean thermal regime of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], has been estimated at 20 years [am = 20 years]. Throughout their adult lives, females maintain a considerable reproductive output when conditions are favorable. At a body size of 4.5 cm SVL, a typical female is capable of producing on average 186 to 1236 eggs per year [Ri = 186 to 1236 eggs per year] at this same 14 °C [T = 14 °C] thermal baseline. The ultimate or asymptotic adult snout-vent length for this species is 5.2 cm [Li = 5.2 cm], though some sources report individuals may reach up to 6 cm under exceptionally favorable conditions. The maximum adult wet weight corresponding to this ultimate body size is 13.9 grams [Wwi = 13.9 grams], a mass that is attained only by the largest, oldest individuals in a population. These life-history metrics place B. bombina at the slower end of the pace-of-life continuum among sympatric anurans.

The reproductive strategy of the European fire-bellied toad is tightly linked to the predictability of its breeding environment. The ability to produce a single, large clutch annually and the relatively long lifespan of two decades [am = two decades] in a cool-temperate climate represent a significant energetic trade-off that must be balanced against the constraints of a short active season. The onset of reproductive activity is deferred until the female reaches a snout-vent length of 4.0 cm [Lp = 4.0 cm] and a weight of 4.1 grams [Wwp = 4.1 grams], a threshold that is not crossed until roughly 1095 days after metamorphosis [tp = roughly 1095 days after metamorphosis] at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. The hatchling mass is minute at 0.0017 grams [Wwb = 0.0017 grams], yet the rapid larval development over 70 days  at 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C] ensures that metamorphosis can be completed within a single favorable season. The newly emerged tadpole, at a total length of 0.7 cm [Lb = 0.7 cm], faces intense size-dependent mortality, a selective pressure that shapes the entire life history of this resilient anuran.
